To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) individual differences in intra-individual variability in a response inhibition paradigm are related to the efficiency with which inhibitory control is implemented and 2) that these differences in performance variability correlate with the extent to which the brain activates inhibitory control networks.

(1) individual differences in response variability were a strong behavioural correlate of response inhibition performance; (2) response time variability was a strong predictor of task-related brain activity in a distributed inhibitory control network; (3) the behavioural and fMR data are consistent with a greater need for top-down executive processes in subjects with relatively high response time variability; and (4) these findings may be relevant to clinical populations with deficits in executive control.
